blocks.content: 1 · What psychological assessment is — and is not

content.text: "a quick search for which DSM diagnosis fits". The lecture listed four typical pitfalls, each with a better alternative:
"Counting" the number of symptoms without meaning
Reducing the client to a label

A student says: "I can't concentrate, I sleep badly and I've lost interest in everything." A rushed clinician counts: 3 symptoms… plus sad mood and fatigue = 5 → "depression". A good clinician first asks:
What do you want help with? Since when? What happened around that time?
Maybe her father became seriously ill two months ago and she is also working nights. Same symptoms — very different picture and very different help.
The working definition for this course:
"Psychological assessment involves a systematic and scientifically informed approach to determining the best possible solution for the client's specific situation."

blocks.content: 7 · Why classifications can be useful — and why they carry risks

content.text: The client's suffering gets a name and is taken seriously.
"What I am experiencing has a name and is taken seriously."
"So I'm not just lazy or weak — there's actually a word for what I have."
A diagnosis may be required to access specialised care, support, or reimbursement (insurance).
"With this classification I can refer you to specialised mental health care, and your insurance will cover the treatment."
Professionals use a shared language to transfer information.
"The client meets the criteria for panic disorder with agoraphobia."
— the colleague immediately knows what kind of problem is meant.
Classifications help organise and standardise research and clinical guidelines.
"For social anxiety disorder, the guideline recommends cognitive behavioural therapy as the first-line treatment."
The person is seen as "the disorder".
"Don't take her complaints too seriously, she's a borderline."
"I'm just a depressive person, that's who I am."
Normal variation or understandable responses are too quickly pathologised (turned into illness).
"My father died three weeks ago and I still cry every day — does that mean I have a depressive disorder?"
"He can't sit still for a whole school day, so he must have ADHD."
What counts as "normal" varies across historical, cultural, and contextual settings.
"He has four symptoms instead of five, so officially it's not depression — even though he can barely get out of bed."
"In my culture, hearing the voice of a relative who died is a normal part of grieving."
Two people with the same diagnosis can have completely different patterns, resources, and goals (
"Both my clients have 'depression', but one lost her job and can't sleep, and the other sleeps twelve hours a day and misses her home country."

The two dominant classification systems: DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association) and ICD-11 (World Health Organization).

Symptom-based categories, based on consensus. They describe criteria: symptoms, duration, severity, distress and impairment.

Used for classification, shared language, access to care, research and treatment.

They do not explain why the problem developed or persists in this person, and they do not provide a diagnosis. Risks: stigma, overmedicalisation, arbitrary boundaries, loss of context.

props.label: Model in a nutshell — Spearman two-factor theory (Spores, 2022)

content.text:
intelligence = one general factor g + specific factors s.
•

g explains roughly 50% of the variance of specific tests; the rest is s + error.
•
supported by positive correlations between tests; one number cannot describe a whole person.

props.label: Model in a nutshell — Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc model (Spores, 2022)

content.text:
hierarchical model with broad abilities under g.
•

Cattell and Horn, as described by Spores.
•

two second-order factors: fluid (Gf) and crystallised (Gc) intelligence.
•

Gf = abstract reasoning, culture-free, capacity to learn. Gc = acquired knowledge and skills. Extended to 10 broad factors; Gf correlates most with g, CDS least.
•
Cattell and Horn played g down; Carroll kept it on top.

props.label: Model in a nutshell — Carroll three-stratum model (Spores, 2022)

content.text:
a model of intelligence in three levels.
•

Carroll (1993), from a reanalysis of more than 461 data sets.
•

Stratum III = g, Stratum II = 8 broad abilities, Stratum I = narrow abilities.
•
Carroll kept g at the top, unlike Cattell-Horn. Vernon (1965) was an earlier hierarchy.

props.label: Model in a nutshell — CHC theory (Spores, 2022)

content.text:
integration of Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc and Carroll's three strata.
•

three strata: g at Stratum III, broad factors at Stratum II, narrow abilities at Stratum I.
•

16 broad factors in the 2012 version (10 Cattell-Horn, 8 Carroll).
•
main driver of modern IQ tests: subtests (narrow) -> index scores (broad) -> FSIQ (g).

props.label: Model in a nutshell — Wechsler interpretation, general to specific (Spores, 2022)

content.text:
Spores' stepwise procedure for interpreting an intelligence test (Figure 7.1).
•

always go from general to specific, and only go deeper when the case needs it.
•

1 FSIQ (with CI near a boundary). 2 Index scores, norm-based. 3 Optional ipsative pairwise comparisons at .01, then base rates. 4 Subtests only if the index is very/extremely low, the subtests clearly differ and it matters.
•
subtests are less reliable (fewer items), so they are treated with suspicion.

Event, thought, feeling, behaviour, consequence (gebeurtenis, gedachten, gevoel, gedrag, gevolg).
The three outcomes of testing a hypothesis: supported (accept), inconclusive so kept open for further assessment (retain), or ruled out (reject).
A standardised, structured observation instrument used in autism assessment.
The last step of the diagnostic cycle: telling the client what you found and agreeing on what happens next. The advice is the
A thinking error: sticking to your first impression and adjusting too little when new information comes in.
The line between “normal” and “disorder” is partly a choice and varies across history, culture and context.
The history as told by the client themselves.
A thinking error: you more readily consider explanations that easily come to mind.
— the NIP's basic registration in psychological assessment; it guarantees a basic level of knowledge and experience in general assessment.
How often a score difference or pattern occurs in the norm group. Rare = more diagnostic weight.
In a network: a symptom that connects two problem clusters (important in comorbidity).
Combining all diagnostic information into one coherent picture of the client (see integrative formulation).
A real cause-effect link. Needs temporal order, a plausible mechanism + research, and alternatives ruled out.
In a network: a symptom with many or strong connections. Central does not automatically mean cause.
Cattell-Horn-Carroll: a hierarchy of cognitive abilities (g → broad abilities → narrow abilities). The most supported theory; basis of WISC/WAIS.
The client's exact age (years; months; days) on the test date. Determines which norm table you use.
The outcome of the complaint analysis: organised and prioritised complaints and help-seeking questions.
Placing symptoms into a category of a system like DSM or ICD. It describes; it does not explain. Classification ≠ diagnosis.
The person to whom the psychological assessment pertains.
The report for non-professionals: same content as the technical report, adapted language (“questions for assessment” instead of “hypotheses”), eight chapters.
The group of people the assessment pertains to, e.g. a client and partner, or a child and parent.
A name for a group of problems that belong together (e.g. “mood problems”) in ordering and labelling.
Help is sought under pressure (parent, partner, employer, school, justice system), which affects openness.
Information from people around the client (partner, parents, significant others). Same as hetero-anamnesis.
The rule, set in advance, for accepting a hypothesis when several instruments are used together.
The person or party that formally commissions the assessment (an external party or the client).
A third factor that causes both variables, so they correlate without one causing the other.
Two or more problems or disorders occurring together in one person.
A subjective thought, feeling, behaviour or (experience of an) event that the client experiences as disturbing, problematic, unwanted or limiting.
Clarifying the client's experience of the problem and the help-seeking questions, in their own language.
Turning vague words into a specific situation: event, thoughts, feeling, behaviour, consequence.
A variable that, according to scientific evidence, triggers or maintains a problem.
The range in which the true score probably lies (e.g. 95% CI 107–118). A score is not an exact point.
A thinking error: looking for information that supports your first hypothesis.
Calmly and hypothetically pointing out a discrepancy, while acceptance stays tangible.
Your words, tone and attitude match. Part of genuineness.
Conversation aimed at reaching agreement, e.g. about the recommendation.
A more specific function within an RDoC domain, e.g. acute threat, reward learning, working memory.
Reasons a treatment does not fit (yet): age, developmental stage, burden.
Using acquired knowledge and experience to solve problems (language, concepts, general knowledge).
Delivering care in the person's own environment instead of in a large institution.

The model of De Bruyn et al. (2003) for systematic assessment: referral → complaint analysis → (scenario) → problem analysis → explanatory analysis → indication analysis → advice/feedback → reporting.
The plan after the complaint analysis: which diagnostic questions and phases the assessment will cover (not on the slides — see Witteman ch. 3).
Stop a subtest after a set number of consecutive 0-scores.
Coming up with many different possible answers; linked to creativity (Guilford).
The dominant classification systems (APA's DSM-5-TR; WHO's ICD-11). Symptom-based, consensus-based categories.
Understanding someone from their lived experience and showing that you understand.
Self-monitoring several times a day in daily life (e.g. via an app like m-Path).
Utility × probability, each rated 0–10; the treatment with the highest product is the most promising.
The phase in which you formulate and test explanations (conditions) for the problems and build an integrative formulation.
Symptoms or factors that keep each other going (a vicious cycle).
Reasoning and solving new problems without relying on prior knowledge.
Rising average test scores across generations; old norms overestimate IQ.
Full-Scale IQ: the global summary score of a Wechsler test (M = 100, SD = 15).
General mental ability that partly explains performance across many cognitive tasks (Spearman).
Privacy law: what information you record and with whom you share it.
Being human and professional: reduce role behaviour, congruence, tactful spontaneity.
Sensitive information often only comes out later, as trust grows.
What the client (or system/referrer) wants from the assessment, ideally in their own words.
The history as told by an informant (parent, partner, teacher).
People with the same diagnosis can differ a lot in symptoms, functioning and mechanisms.
Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology: a dimensional, hierarchical, data-driven model of symptoms and spectra.
Harm caused by the care itself (e.g. a label that makes someone feel more stuck).
A responsible, scientifically grounded recommendation for the most appropriate approach to the problem; the basis of the advisory phase.
The phase in which you decide which help/treatment fits (Lecture 9).
Reasons a treatment fits this client: strong motivation, openness to critical reflection, ability to verbalise thoughts, resources such as social support.
Different, cognitively diverse task sets approximate the same g.
Conversation aimed at influencing or changing the client's behaviour; in the advisory interview it appears at the consultation about the recommendation.
Conversation aimed at exchanging, conveying and gathering information.
Explicit agreement at the start about time, goal, roles and space.
Integration of all results in relation to the help question, complaints and problems = the explanatory diagnosis.
A person related to the assessment who is informed of the outcome (employer, partner, GP).
A hidden cause assumed to produce the observed symptoms (the DSM view the network approach rejects).
The Dutch statutory statement establishing that you meet the admission requirements of the healthcare performance model.
A middle step through which X affects Y (X → M → Y).
Mean Index Score: average of the primary index scores; a comparison score for strengths and weaknesses.
A variable that changes the strength or direction of the X → Y relationship.
Mean Scaled Score of the primary subtests; comparison score at subtest level.
Comparing many scores makes a chance “finding” likely; use hypotheses set in advance.
Sees psychopathology as symptoms that directly influence and maintain each other.
In a network: node = a symptom or factor; edge = the connection between two nodes (positive or negative).
The comparison group a test's scores are based on; must fit the client and the intended use.
Offering a possible connection in a questioning tone (“I wonder whether… how do you see that?”).
Make a condition observable and choose how to measure it.
Turning the condition named in a hypothesis into something observable and measurable.
Goals about the change the client wants; ownership mainly with the client.
Exaggerating complaints to get help, recognition or urgency.
The general factor of psychopathology at the top of the HiTOP hierarchy.
Repeating the content of what the client said in your own words.
Looking for the interactions that maintain a problem (problem-sustaining patterns).
The % of the norm group that scored lower (e.g. 81st percentile = higher than 81%).
Cognitive tasks generally correlate positively — the evidence for g.
Giving problem behaviour a new, more constructive label.
Propositions about the conditions that led to or maintain this client's problem; can be drawn as a scheme.
Too quickly treating a complaint as a cause or disorder.
The intelligence level someone probably had before an illness or brain injury (estimated with e.g. the NLV).
The chance that a treatment succeeds with this client, judged on the indication and contraindication criteria.
From subjective to objective: describe, order/label and assess the severity of the problems.
A dynamic pattern of bio-psycho-social interactions that persistently or recurrently undermines everyday problem-solving.
Goals about how the conversation goes (calm, trust, space); mainly the practitioner's responsibility.
Strengths and resources that reduce risk or severity (support, skills, network).
Research Domain Criteria: a transdiagnostic research framework of functional domains × units of analysis.
The first phase: who comes, why now, with which question — brief basic information.
The professional who, within a professional relationship, advised the client about assessment (GP, psychiatrist).
The person who first contacts the care provider (client, GP, partner…).
Naming the feeling or meaning behind the client's words.
Treating a disorder label as if it were a real “thing” inside the person.
How free a score is from measurement error.
Go back to easier items when the start level wasn't established.
The supposed effect is (also) the cause, e.g. depression ↔ poor sleep.
Ten questions (1975) to judge the severity of a problem behaviour.
A professional who combines scientific, systematic reasoning with practice.
Sharing something about yourself; only if functional, relevant, measured, and the focus returns to the client.
The client observes and records their own behaviour (thought record, ESM).
Giving advice before the problem and help question are clear.
Start with the lightest suitable help; “step up” when needed.
Zubin & Spring (1977): the higher the vulnerability, the less stress needed to become ill.
An ordered overview of the main points; checks understanding and structures the talk.
An “explanation” that just repeats the problem with a label (“sad because depressed”).
The report for colleagues and supervisors: every step and its reasoning, full detail on sources, instruments, psychometrics and results, following the NIP codes.
The standard used in a research method to decide whether a hypothesis can be accepted; without it, testing is of little use.
A standard, set in advance, that decides whether a hypothesis is accepted.
Sharing your reasoning: “I notice… I wonder… how do you see that?”
Relevant across many disorders (e.g. rumination, neuroticism).
Seeing the client as a person of value and dignity; acceptance, not approval.
Minimising complaints out of shame, fear, resistance or loyalty.
The positive and negative outcomes of a treatment, based on effectiveness, matching and coverage.
The evidence that a score supports the interpretation and decision you make.
